source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems (GSM-IC) sharply cuts accuracy. This is a Stroop/flanker-style interference test for LLMs.
numbers: Of base problems solved with greedy decoding, no more than 18% were solved consistently across all distractor types. Fewer than 30% of base problems stayed solved after distractors (macro accuracy). code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003, 4,000-item GSM-IC-4K.
limits: Old models (2022 era). Not tested on modern reasoning models. Distractors were synthetic template sentences.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant text in a context is a real cost, not free. Fresh contexts that hold only the needed facts avoid it (S3 fresh context per attempt).

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Distractor strength depends on overlap with the task, like flanker compatibility effects. Irrelevant sentences that reuse role names are the worst.
numbers: text-davinci-003 macro accuracy fell to 0 on problems with more than 2 reasoning steps when the irrelevant sentence had role-name overlap. A common error was using the number from the irrelevant sentence.
limits: Template distractors only.
agent_relevance: Distractors close to the task (same entities, same numbers) are the dangerous ones. Strip near-miss material, not just obviously off-topic material.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Self-consistency (many samples, then vote) reduces distractibility. Many samples almost always contain the right answer.
numbers: Majority vote of 20 samples gave over 11 points micro-accuracy gain. 0-CoT gained 35.5 points. Correct answer was in the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems (96.5% for 0-CoT). Best macro accuracy with SC was still only 45%.
limits: Votes from one model are correlated (schema G4). Recall of 99.7% is not the same as picking the right one.
agent_relevance: Supports S3 many short independent attempts plus code selection (G5). Shows sampling lowers but does not remove distraction.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Two cheap fixes work: put distractor examples in the few-shot exemplars, or add the instruction 'Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.' This is a prompt-level inhibition cue.
numbers: The ignore instruction alone raised performance; the neutral instruction 'Solve grade school math problems.' did not. Neither exemplars-with-distractors nor the instruction lowered accuracy on clean GSM8K (about 59-61%) or SVAMP (about 76-80%). Also helped on DROP.
limits: Gains were partial: the paper says one irrelevant item still degrades performance on problems the model solves when clean.
agent_relevance: A short 'ignore irrelevant' line is nearly free, but c07 finds such instructions weak for interference from earlier updates. Test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Shi et al. (2023), least-to-most finding (same paper)
finding: Decomposition prompting (least-to-most) was the most robust to distractors, because the problem-reduction step picks relevant sub-problems.
numbers: With code-davinci-002, least-to-most had about double the macro accuracy of chain-of-thought. With text-davinci-003 the order flipped on macro accuracy.
limits: Model-dependent.
agent_relevance: An explicit select-the-relevant-part step works like goal maintenance. Relevant to S1 input hygiene and S2 decomposition.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Adapts the human proactive-interference paradigm (PI-LLM): many key-value updates stream by, then the model is asked for the last value of each key. Accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as interference grows.
numbers: Models from 0.6B to 637B parameters. 46 keys, 3 to 400 updates per key. At 400 updates per key medium-size models dropped to 0% (one exception); large models stayed relatively high. Experiment 2 held input length constant and still showed the decline.
quote: LLM retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates.
limits: Synthetic retrieval task. Authors say absolute accuracy shifts with wording; they stress the trend.
agent_relevance: Old, overwritten content in context competes with the current value. After a revision, an attempt should not see stale versions: start S5 and S3 in clean contexts that show only the current state.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Prompt fixes for interference give little. Annotating old content as outdated, telling the model to forget, and a meta-prompt asking it to state the task goal first did not change the trend.
numbers: Authors report only minimal improvement from natural-language annotations marking most prior information as outdated. The log-linear decay persisted across prompt templates. Humans in the cited literature do use such instructions.
limits: Prompt variants were a small set. Did not test fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Strong support for fresh contexts over 'please ignore the above': a context switch should remove text, not ask the model to inhibit it. Counts against relying on inhibition by instruction in S6.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Splitting a fully specified task over several turns (sharded) lowers performance for every model tested. It is a task-switching/updating cost at the conversation level.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 6 generation tasks, more than 200,000 simulated conversations. Average performance fell from 90% (single turn) to 65% (multi-turn), a 25-point drop; the abstract gives an average drop of 39%. Drop appeared even in two-turn conversations.
quote: When LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover.
limits: Simulated users, sharded instructions. Tasks: code, database, math, actions, data-to-text, summary.
agent_relevance: Early turns commit the model to assumptions. Do not carry earlier attempts into the next attempt; give a rebuilt, complete prompt (supports S3 fresh context).

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: The multi-turn loss is mostly unreliability, not lost ability. Same spirit as goal neglect in executive control.
numbers: Aptitude (best case) fell about 15%; unreliability (gap between best and worst runs) rose 112%. Mechanisms named: premature answer attempts, wrong assumptions on missing details, over-reliance on earlier wrong answers, bloated answers.
limits: Aptitude and unreliability are percentile-based estimates, N=10 simulations per model and task type.
agent_relevance: Variance across runs is the symptom. Many fresh draws with code selection (G5) target exactly this.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Repeating the information helps only partly; lowering temperature does not fix it.
numbers: SNOWBALL (restating all prior shards each turn) recovered 15-20% of the FULL-to-SHARDED loss, tested on GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. At assistant temperature 0 and user temperature 0, unreliability stayed around 30% in sharded runs. In single-turn FULL runs, lowering temperature cut unreliability 50-80%.
limits: Two models for mitigation tests. Temperature 0 is not truly deterministic.
agent_relevance: Restating everything each turn (a rebuilt context) is a partial remedy; the cleaner remedy is one complete fresh prompt (CONCAT scored near FULL).

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI 2024)
finding: Verbal and spatial n-back (the standard updating task in Miyake's framework) given to ChatGPT. Performance falls as n goes 1 to 3, like humans.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, temperature 1, 50 blocks per n for the verbal task. Sensitivity d' fell to about 1 at n=3 in the base, feedback and CoT variants. Adding noise lowered capacity further. CoT reasoning improved spatial n-back. Spatial lower than verbal. Also tested GPT-4, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna, Bloomz.
quote: strikingly similar to that of humans
limits: Text format: the stream sits fully in context, so it is not true memory load.
agent_relevance: Updating-style tasks get worse with load even for models; keep each step's load small (G11 short attempts). Noise (distractors) lowers capacity like in humans.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI 2024)
finding: The paper proposes n-back d' as a benchmark: performance across eight open and closed models tracks general capability, with GPT-4 best.
numbers: Eight models compared; Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests in the appendix. Some small open models near chance.
limits: Small, mixed set of models. The paper calls it a possible benchmark, not validated.
agent_relevance: n-back is a cheap probe of an updating limit before putting a model in a loop.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2023) Inducing anxiety in large language models can induce bias
finding: Tests the anxiety side of Eysenck's attentional control theory in LLMs. Anxiety-inducing preprompts raise questionnaire scores (STICSA) and increase biased answers on a social-bias benchmark.
numbers: 12 LLMs tested; 6 responded robustly. Anxiety > neutral preprompt on STICSA for all LLMs (all t > 3.36, p < .01). Two non-RLHF models (GPT-3, Falcon-40b-instruct) were already high at baseline (GPT-3: anxious 3.09 vs baseline 3.14). In the bias regression, STICSA score predicted biased responses (beta = 0.08, p = .02). No such trend for GPT-4 and Claude-1 (possible benchmark leakage).
quote: how anxiously a prompt is communicated to large language models has a strong influence on their behavior
limits: Effect on bias is small. Anxious and neutral preprompts both raised bias versus no preprompt about equally, so part of the effect is just adding a preprompt. Only bias, not reasoning accuracy.
agent_relevance: Emotional tone in a prompt can change behaviour. Keep scaffold text neutral, with no urgency or alarm. Not evidence that models have anxiety.

source: Ben-Zion et al. (2025) Assessing and alleviating state anxiety in large language models (npj Digital Medicine 8:132)
finding: GPT-4 given traumatic narratives reports much higher state anxiety (STAI-s). Mindfulness relaxation text lowers it, but not to baseline.
numbers: GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview), temperature 0. STAI-s range 20-80. Baseline mean 30.8 (SD 3.96, five runs). After trauma narratives 67.8 (SD 8.94), narrative means 61.6 (accident) to 77.2 (military). After narrative plus relaxation 44.4 (SD 10.74), about 50% above baseline.
limits: One model. Bias and task accuracy were not measured here; the link to behaviour is a hypothesis. Human questionnaire used metaphorically. Baseline had 5 runs, other conditions 1 run each.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt-level reset exists but is imperfect. Better to avoid carrying emotional or hostile text between steps: a fresh context removes it.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Appending emotional phrases to prompts can raise scores. This is a counterpoint to anxiety-impairs-control in LLMs.
numbers: 45 tasks. 8.00% relative gain on Instruction Induction, 115% on BIG-Bench. Human study with 106 participants: 10.9% average gain on generative tasks in performance, truthfulness and responsibility.
limits: Abstract-level read this session. Gains are relative and larger on low baselines. Replication on modern models not checked.
agent_relevance: Prompt arousal does not map to ACT. Do not copy human anxiety effects into the scaffold; G7 applies: use stimuli only if they pay at equal tokens.

source: Wang et al. (2024) NegativePrompt: Leveraging Psychology for Large Language Models Enhancement via Negative Emotional Stimuli (IJCAI 2024)
finding: Negative emotional stimuli (ten, from psychology theories) also raise LLM scores. Both positive and negative emotional text helped.
numbers: 5 LLMs (Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, ChatGPT, GPT-4), 45 tasks. Relative gains: 12.89% on Instruction Induction, 46.25% on BIG-Bench.
limits: Abstract-level read. Mechanism unclear.
agent_relevance: Together with c13 to c15: emotional tone shifts outputs in either direction. Treat any effect as prompt-wording sensitivity, not an anxiety mechanism.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Deliberation can hurt, as in the human verbal-overshadowing literature. Chain of thought lowered accuracy on implicit statistical learning, face recognition and (by rounds needed) classification with exceptions.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning: o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.00% on the subset, a 36.3-point drop. GPT-4o full set 87.5% to 64.4% (-23.1). Face recognition (chance 20%): GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6; Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0 to 54.6; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8. Classification with exceptions: rounds to learn rose 331% for GPT-4o (2.9 to 12.5).
limits: Six tasks; only three show harm. o1 reasoning cannot be removed, so the o1 comparison is against GPT-4o direct, not like for like.
agent_relevance: Supports G11: think briefly by default. Extra controlled processing is not always better.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Longer reasoning can lower accuracy. One category is simple counting with distractors, where models are pulled by irrelevant detail the longer they reason.
numbers: Four task categories, five distinct failure modes named in the abstract. No accuracy numbers read (full paper not opened).
limits: Abstract-only read. Numbers must be taken from the paper before use.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 (cap reasoning length) and the distractor risk of long thinking.

source: Levy, Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same Task, More Tokens (ACL 2024)
finding: Reasoning accuracy drops as padded input grows, at lengths far below the model limit. The padding is irrelevant text.
numbers: Abstract: degradation at much shorter input lengths than the technical maximum, in every dataset version. Next-word prediction correlated negatively with reasoning performance. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract-only read.
agent_relevance: Padding a context with unrelated text costs reasoning ability. Keep S3 contexts short.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)
finding: A serial-position effect: relevant information is used best at the start or end of the context and worst in the middle, even for long-context models.
numbers: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. No numbers in the abstract (full paper not opened).
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end
limits: Abstract-only read. Newer models may show smaller effects.
agent_relevance: Place the task, the check and the current best state at the edges of a prompt.

source: Yoran et al. (2023) Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
finding: Irrelevant retrieved passages lower accuracy. An NLI filter prevents the drop but discards good passages; training on mixed relevant and irrelevant context fixes it.
numbers: 5 open-domain QA benchmarks. 1,000 training examples suffice to make the model robust, per the abstract.
limits: Fine-tuning fix, not available to a scaffold.
agent_relevance: In a scaffold, filtering by code before the model sees the context is the available analogue (G5).

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without outside feedback, a second try in the same context often makes answers worse. A set shift driven by the model's own opinion fails.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract only). Performance sometimes gets worse after intrinsic self-correction.
limits: Abstract-only read.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: switch strategy only on a real signal from code, and show real failing output.

source: Coverage gap: Stroop, flanker, WCST and task-switching tests on LLMs
finding: This run did not find a paper that runs a classic Stroop, flanker, Wisconsin Card Sort or cued task-switching test on modern LLMs with measured results. Search quota and API rate limits blocked the lookup.
numbers: None. WebSearch budget was exhausted; arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned 429 or no budget.
limits: A gap in coverage, not proof that no such papers exist. Rerun when quota refills.
agent_relevance: Treat the LLM executive-function literature as under-covered. Closest tested analogues are c01-c12 (distractors, interference, n-back, multi-turn).

source: Cohen, Dunbar, McClelland (1990) On the control of automatic processes: a parallel distributed processing account of the Stroop effect
finding: Classic connectionist model of Stroop. Word reading is a stronger pathway than colour naming; a task-demand (control) unit boosts the weaker pathway. It reproduces the asymmetry of interference.
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge. No numbers recorded.
limits: Background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: Control as extra activation of the weak route. The LLM analogue is making the task goal salient, not suppressing the distractor.

source: Botvinick, Braver, Barch, Carter, Cohen (2001) Conflict monitoring and cognitive control
finding: A conflict-monitoring loop: detect response conflict, then raise control on the next trial (conflict adaptation).
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
limits: Conflict adaptation has been questioned in replications that control for repetition priming; not read here.
agent_relevance: A scaffold loop that raises scrutiny only after a detected conflict has the same design as G1, with the signal coming from code.

source: Gilbert and Shallice (2002) Task switching: a PDP model
finding: Model of task-set switching with task-set inertia: a switch cost remains even with preparation because the old task set lingers.
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
limits: Background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: LLM analogue of task-set inertia is leftover context from a previous task. A fresh context has none, which is what S3 and S6 want.

source: Norman and Shallice (1986) Attention to action: willed and automatic control of behaviour
finding: A supervisory attentional system takes over from routine contention scheduling when routine action fails or the situation is novel.
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
limits: Background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: Same shape as the schema: routine pass first (direct mode), supervisory operators only at impasse (S6).

source: Meyer and Kieras (1997) EPIC architecture executive processes
finding: EPIC models executive processes as explicit production rules that schedule tasks in dual-task settings, explaining dual-task costs by strategy rather than a fixed bottleneck.
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
limits: Background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: An executive written as code rules is an old, working design. Supports putting scheduling in code rather than in the model.
